subject: Pediatrics
subtopic: Clinical picture, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis of inherited and acquired hemolysis
concept: Pediatric hemolytic anemia results from shortened red-cell survival with marrow compensation when possible. Important childhood disorders include sickle cell disease, thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency and immune hemolysis.

content.definition: Hemolytic anemia occurs when red-cell destruction exceeds effective production. Hemolysis may be intravascular or extravascular and inherited or acquired.
content.explanation: Typical clues include anemia with reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, elevated LDH and reduced haptoglobin when appropriate. Splenomegaly is common in extravascular hemolysis. The exact presentation depends on the disorder: sickle cell disease causes vaso-occlusion and hemolysis; thalassemia causes ineffective erythropoiesis and chronic anemia; hereditary spherocytosis causes membrane-related extravascular hemolysis; G6PD deficiency can cause episodic oxidative hemolysis.
content.mechanism: Increased red-cell destruction stimulates erythropoietin and marrow reticulocytosis. In sickle cell disease, HbS polymerization under deoxygenation promotes sickling, hemolysis and vaso-occlusion. In thalassemia, reduced globin-chain synthesis causes ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis.
content.structure: Evaluation combines CBC, reticulocyte count, smear, bilirubin, LDH and haptoglobin with targeted testing. Hemoglobin analysis by electrophoresis/HPLC helps identify hemoglobinopathies. Family history and genetic testing may be useful. Direct antiglobulin testing helps evaluate immune hemolysis.
content.function: Hemolysis lowers oxygen-carrying capacity and may cause jaundice, pigment gallstones, splenomegaly and compensatory reticulocytosis.
causes: Hereditary spherocytosis and other membrane disorders
effects: Pain crises and acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease
Growth and endocrine complications in severe transfusion-dependent thalassemia
content.clinical_relevance: Pediatric hemolytic anemia requires recognition of acute complications and long-term complications. Inherited disorders need family counseling and longitudinal care.
content.diagnosis: Confirm hemolysis with a compatible laboratory pattern, then identify the cause. Smear may reveal spherocytes or sickling-related changes; hemoglobin analysis is important for hemoglobinopathies; enzyme or membrane testing is selected according to the suspected disorder. In G6PD deficiency, testing can be falsely reassuring during or shortly after hemolysis because young reticulocytes contain more enzyme.
content.treatment: Treatment is disorder-specific. Sickle cell disease management includes disease-modifying therapy such as hydroxyurea, infection prevention, pain and acute complication management, transfusion when indicated, and selected curative cellular or gene therapies. Severe transfusion-dependent thalassemia is managed with regular RBC transfusions and iron-overload monitoring/chelation. Hereditary spherocytosis may require folate support and, in selected patients, splenectomy; G6PD deficiency centers on trigger avoidance and supportive care. Immune hemolysis requires treatment of the immune cause and severity-guided therapy.
high_yield: Reticulocytosis is a key clue to marrow compensation in hemolysis.
Sickle cell disease is diagnosed using hemoglobin testing and may be confirmed with genetic testing.
Severe thalassemia may require regular transfusions and iron chelation.
Do not give iron simply because a patient with thalassemia is anemic unless iron deficiency is independently demonstrated.
G6PD assays may need repeat testing after an acute hemolytic episode if the initial result is not definitive.
